newsitem.title: USA: Delta pilots seek wage increase, airline chief to retire.
newsitem.headline: Delta pilots seek wage increase, airline chief to retire.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. said Monday that Chief Executive Ronald Allen will retire and resign from the board of directors when his contract expires on July 31.
Separately, Delta's pilots said they will seek pay raises and work rule changes only a year after ratifying the current four-year contract with the nation's third-largest airline.
The pilots' demands were driven by Delta's turnaround to record third-quarter profits and recent pay raises for non-union employees, spurred by union sacrifices under Allen's tenure.
"Recent events at both our company and in our industry raise serious questions about the fairness and equity of maintaining the status quo," they said.
The pilots did not provide specific wage goals or work rule changes.

Analysts said the pilots' efforts may be hampered as Delta seeks a new chief. Allen, 55, who is also chairman and president of the carrier, will work with the board to find a successor and remain as a consultant and advisory director.

Delta also named Maurice Worth, executive vice president of customer service, as acting chief operating officer. Worth, 56, has 36 years of service at Delta in operations, station management and personnel.
Worth is one of three executive vice presidents at Delta who serve as members of the Executive Council with Allen. The Executive Council was formed in 1995 to set corporate policy and strategy.

Delta's pilots ratified a four-year contract in April 1996. Its provisions included a 2 percent pay cut in return for stock options, a profit-sharing plan comparable to those enjoyed by other Delta employees, a seat on the Atlanta-based company's board and improved retirement benefits.
At the time, Delta said it expected to save more than $750 million over the four years as a result of the collective bargaining agreement with the pilots.
Delta's pilots now contend that the situation has changed.

"When we entered into our contract a year ago, the pilots made a collective decision to accept major changes to our working agreement in an effort to assist ... in making Delta more competitive and to return the company to sustained profitability," the union's master executive council said in a recorded message to the pilots.

"Delta management has now consciously altered both their revenue and cost-cutting goals and has announced a much-deserved pay raise for non-contract employees. Against this backdrop, it is time to reconsider the pilots' level of participation needed to accomplish management's now-modified goals," the union said.

The Delta pilots also said there is a "growing disparity between Delta's pilot compensation and the compensation of our peers in the industry -- a disparity that will significantly increase over the next few years."

Pilots at American Airlines recently ratified a five-year labour contract that offered a 9 percent wage increase. Pilots at United Airlines also approved a proposal that includes two mid-term wage increases of 5 percent.
Delta's stock rose $1.25 to $95.75 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
